title.narrative: Reducing spatial inequalities for vulnerable youth in Iraq

description.narrative:
The rise and fall of the so-called Islamic State (ISIL) in Iraq have been especially destructive for adolescents and youth recruited and exploited by the group. As a result of their alleged association with the terrorist group, numerous young Iraqis are currently ostracised, with many deprived of their liberty. This is cause for special concern by Iraqi authorities and the society at large. According to figures provided by national authorities in 2019, detention facilities across the country host over 2,000 boys and girls 'perceived as' being associated with ISIL. Those who are suspected of terrorism-related activities are usually arrested and detained by the security forces or intelligence actors under the Federal Anti-Terrorism Law of 2005, but there is a limited practical experience on how to deal specifically with youth who are perceived as being associated and affiliated with this group. The impact of detention is devastating for them. They are separated from their families and communities for long stretches of time, and many become even more vulnerable during their detention. Furthermore, detained adolescents and youth most often face stigma upon returning to their communities, as they are labelled as 'terrorists' or 'violent extremists'.
Due to extensive physical damage and the financial requirements to rebuild Iraqi cities after the conflict with ISIL, progress is slow and complex. Investments in social reconciliation and peace-building are limited. Political dynamics further hamper the implementation of crucial activities required to protect and serve vulnerable adolescents and youth. Currently, the justice sector is overwhelmed by the massive caseloads and warrants for arrests. In Mosul alone, there are currently more than thousands of young people in detention under the Ministry of Interior (MOI), the majority under the terrorism law, out of which, only a fraction has been sentenced. The rest remains under investigation.
National authorities have requested assistance to tackle the situation of young people who are currently in detention for alleged affiliation/association with terrorist groups and to strengthen current efforts to promote their rehabilitation and reintegration. There is a need to support judicial authorities in improving the conditions of detention and the treatment of young people deprived of their liberty as a pre-requirement for rehabilitation and reintegration efforts. In parallel, the justice system itself should enable rehabilitation and reintegration processes, ensure fair legal treatment, and provide the necessary skills to the personnel of detention facilities and reformatories to better serve and protect young people.
